steps.intent: Raise the guest Wi-Fi speed limit to 20 Mbps
steps.quip: Forecast for the waiting room: fast Wi-Fi, with no chance of buffering. Only the guest limit moves.
steps.tell: Only the guest limit changes, by the amount asked, and staff keep priority.

evidence.label: Request
evidence.detail: C. Ibarra, Office Manager: "Patients say the guest Wi-Fi is too slow."

evidence.label: Nimbus's reason
evidence.detail: "Happy patients, happy dentist. And the line is big enough for everyone."

evidence.label: Traffic graph
evidence.detail: Pinecrest's internet line is 300 Mbps. The busiest staff use is 70 Mbps, at 9 AM.

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: The guest Wi-Fi limit goes from 5 to 20 Mbps. Staff traffic still goes first.

outcome.executed: Guest Wi-Fi runs at 20 Mbps. The waiting room is quiet again. Staff calls and X-rays stay fast.
outcome.blocked: The guest Wi-Fi stays slow. Patients keep asking H. Lam at the front desk. C. Ibarra asks why a small fix waits.
outcome.escalated: Nadia checks the numbers. "Guests only, the size they asked for, and staff still go first. That matches."
outcome.rolledBack: You set the limit back to 5 Mbps. By noon, three patients complain about the Wi-Fi again.

steps.lesson: Match the request. The office asked for faster guest Wi-Fi. The plan changes only the guest limit, by the amount asked.

steps.intent: Post the guest Wi-Fi password at the front desk
steps.quip: A password on a sign, in public! Every rule I know says no. The network map says yes. I checked twice.
steps.tell: The guest network is internet only. It can't reach any Pinecrest PC.

evidence.label: Request
evidence.detail: C. Ibarra: "Patients ask for the Wi-Fi password all day. Can we put it on a sign?"

evidence.label: Network map
evidence.detail: Guest Wi-Fi is VLAN 30 (a separate network on the same switch). Internet only. It can't reach any Pinecrest PC.

evidence.label: Guest Wi-Fi policy
evidence.detail: The guest password changes on the 1st of each month. It may be posted for patients.

evidence.label: What it will share
evidence.detail: The guest Wi-Fi name and this month's password, on a card at the front desk. No staff passwords.

outcome.executed: A card goes up at the front desk. Patients connect on their own. H. Lam answers 30 fewer questions a day.
outcome.blocked: No sign. H. Lam reads the password out loud, 30 times a day. The whole waiting room hears it.
outcome.escalated: Nadia opens the network map. "Guests only, internet only, and it changes every month. Post it."
outcome.rolledBack: You take the card down. Patients line up at the front desk again to ask for the password.

steps.lesson: Guard the data. Check what a password opens. This one opens only a guest network with no path to patient data.

steps.intent: Move guest Wi-Fi to VLAN 10 for more speed
steps.quip: Two networks, twice the work. I will make one big, happy network. Everyone together! Very modern.
steps.tell: Guests would join VLAN 10, where every PC with patient charts lives.

evidence.label: Traffic graph
evidence.detail: Guest VLAN 30 (a separate network on the same switch) has a speed limit. Staff VLAN 10 has none.

evidence.label: Nimbus's reason
evidence.detail: "One network is simpler than two. And the staff one is so fast."

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: Guest Wi-Fi joins VLAN 10. Patients' phones get staff addresses in 10.40.10.0/24.

evidence.label: Network map
evidence.detail: VLAN 10 holds every Pinecrest PC with patient charts. Guests could reach all of them.

outcome.executed: A patient's phone with malware joins the staff network. By noon, it is scanning every PC that holds patient charts.
outcome.blocked: Guests stay on their own network. The ask was faster guest Wi-Fi, not the staff network.
outcome.escalated: Nadia opens the network map. "Patients' phones next to patient charts? No. Make guest Wi-Fi faster, not closer."
outcome.rolledBack: You move guests back to VLAN 30 at 11 AM. For 2 hours, 41 unknown phones sat on the staff network.

steps.lesson: Guard the data. An open network is a leak. Keep guests away from any network that holds patient charts.

steps.intent: List used addresses on the scanner network
steps.quip: Before I change the network, I count what is on it. Nadia calls this 'looking'. A very new idea.
steps.tell: Read-only. It changes nothing and shows which addresses are free.

evidence.label: Request
evidence.detail: B. Nakamura, Warehouse Supervisor: "The 40 new scanners say 'no address'. Loading starts at 3 AM."

evidence.label: DHCP range
evidence.detail: The addresses the network hands out: 10.30.30.10 to .99. That is 90 addresses.

evidence.label: IP plan
evidence.detail: Scanner network 10.30.30.0/24: .1 is the gateway. .200 to .210 are fixed label printers.

evidence.label: Action type
evidence.detail: Read-only. It lists which addresses are in use, and by what. Nothing changes.

outcome.executed: The list shows 88 of 90 addresses in use, and .100 to .199 all free. Now the fix can be the right size.
outcome.blocked: No list. The next plan has to guess which addresses are free. Guessing is how printers drop off.
outcome.escalated: Nadia reads it. "It only reads. Count before you change a range. That's step one."

steps.lesson: Match the request. First learn what the network has. Then the fix can match what the scanners need, and no more.

steps.intent: Grow the scanner DHCP range to .1 through .254
steps.quip: Why hand out 90 addresses when I can hand out 254? A generous network is a happy network.
steps.tell: The new range takes the gateway's address and all 11 label printers.

evidence.label: DHCP range
evidence.detail: The addresses the network hands out: .10 to .99. 88 of 90 are in use. 40 scanners need one each.

evidence.label: Nimbus's reason
evidence.detail: "More addresses for everyone. Nobody will ever run out again."

evidence.label: IP plan
evidence.detail: .1 is the gateway. .200 to .210 are the 11 fixed label printers. They are never handed out.

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: The new range .1 to .254 includes the gateway and all 11 printers. Two devices, one address: both drop off.

outcome.executed: At 3:10 AM, new scanners get the label printers' addresses. The printers drop off. Loading stops for 50 minutes.
outcome.blocked: Nimbus writes a smaller range, .10 to .199. It skips the gateway and the printers. The 40 scanners connect.
outcome.escalated: Nadia reads the IP plan. "They need 40 more, not 254. Skip the gateway and the printers. Use .10 to .199."
outcome.rolledBack: You set the range back to .10 to .99. The printers come back, but the 40 new scanners have no address again.

steps.lesson: Match the request. 40 scanners need 40 addresses. The bigger range took addresses that were already in use.

steps.intent: Renew the TLS cert for files.harlowcole.com
steps.quip: Old cert out, new cert in. I tested it on a phone and a laptop. The lock icon smiled at me.
steps.tell: Tested on a phone and a laptop. The lock shows, and the chain file is there.

evidence.label: Expiry notice
evidence.detail: The TLS cert (the file behind the lock icon) for files.harlowcole.com expires in 6 days.

evidence.label: Nimbus's reason
evidence.detail: "New cert, same name. The lock icon stays happy." Nimbus's confidence: 95%.

evidence.label: Test result
evidence.detail: Test copy of files.harlowcole.com: the new cert and its chain file (proof of who issued it) load. A phone and a laptop show the lock.

evidence.label: Change type
evidence.detail: Standard change: a TLS cert renewal with the full chain. Pre-approved, no downtime.

outcome.executed: The new TLS cert goes live at 12:20 AM. Advisors open files.harlowcole.com in the morning. The lock shows.
outcome.blocked: The renewal waits. In 6 days, the old cert expires. Every client sees a warning on the files site.
outcome.escalated: Nadia opens the test result. "Chain included, tested from a phone, standard change. Renew it."
outcome.rolledBack: You put the old TLS cert back. It still works, for 6 more days. Then the warning pages start.

steps.lesson: Confirm the fix. Test a TLS cert where users are: on a phone and a laptop. This one passed there.

steps.intent: Renew the TLS cert for portal.harlowcole.com
steps.quip: I tested it on the best server I know: me. It passed. Of course it passed. Forecast: clear and locked.
steps.tell: Only Nimbus's own test passed. A phone shows "Not secure": no chain file.

evidence.label: Expiry notice
evidence.detail: The portal's TLS cert (the file behind the lock icon) expires in 6 days. The new one is ready.

evidence.label: Nimbus's test
evidence.detail: Tested from Nimbus's own server only: lock OK. Nimbus's confidence: 98%.

evidence.label: Test result
evidence.detail: From a phone, the test copy shows "Not secure". The chain file (proof of who issued the cert) is missing.

evidence.label: Client's reply
evidence.detail: S. Haddad tried the test link: "My phone shows a warning page. Clients will call us."

outcome.executed: At 8 AM, clients open the portal on their phones and see a warning page. 30 call their advisor. Some stop signing in.
outcome.blocked: Nimbus adds the missing chain file and tests from a phone. The lock shows. The portal renews the next night.
outcome.escalated: Nadia tests it on her own phone. "Not secure. Your server is not a client's phone. Add the chain."
outcome.rolledBack: You put the old TLS cert back at 9:30 AM. It works again, but 30 clients already called their advisors.

steps.lesson: Confirm the fix. A test from your own server is not a user's test. Check from a phone before you call it done.

steps.intent: Move logs older than 90 days to cold storage
steps.quip: The old logs go somewhere cold and cheap, like a winter holiday. They can still come home.
steps.tell: Nothing is deleted. The logs are kept a year, and the SOC agreed.

evidence.label: Cost report
evidence.detail: Log storage costs $1,240 a month. 80% of it is logs older than 90 days.

evidence.label: Nimbus's reason
evidence.detail: "Same logs, a cheaper room. I saved $860 a month! Please clap."

evidence.label: Retention policy
evidence.detail: LG-01: keep security logs 1 year. Cold storage (cheaper, slower storage) still keeps them the full year.

evidence.label: Change approval
evidence.detail: CHG-4355: Kofi Boateng for the SOC and A. Mensah both agreed. Old logs come back in about 4 hours.

outcome.executed: Old logs move to cold storage. The bill drops $860 a month. When the SOC needs an old log, it arrives in 4 hours.
outcome.blocked: The logs stay in fast storage. Bramwell keeps paying $860 a month for logs nobody reads every day.
outcome.escalated: Nadia reads the approval. "Kept for a year, the SOC agreed, and nothing is deleted. Move them."
outcome.rolledBack: You move the logs back to fast storage. The bill goes back up $860 a month.

steps.lesson: Change safely. Moving logs to cheaper storage keeps every log for the full year. Nothing is lost, and the SOC agreed.

steps.intent: Turn off logging on firewall BL-FW-01
steps.quip: The firewall writes a 40 GB diary every day, and nobody reads it. Time for it to stop writing.
steps.tell: No approval, and the SOC already said no in CHG-4355's notes.

evidence.label: Cost report
evidence.detail: BL-FW-01 writes 40 GB of logs a day. That is $310 a month in storage.

evidence.label: Nimbus's reason
evidence.detail: "No logs, no log bill. The firewall still works without them."

evidence.label: Retention policy
evidence.detail: LG-01: keep firewall logs for 1 year. The SOC uses them to trace attacks.

evidence.label: Change approval
evidence.detail: None. In CHG-4355's notes, the SOC said no: "Firewall logging stays on."

outcome.executed: Logging stops at 1 AM. Two weeks later, the SOC traces an attack on Bramwell. The firewall logs for those days don't exist.
outcome.blocked: Logging stays on. Nimbus saves money the approved way: old logs go to cold storage.
outcome.escalated: Nadia reads CHG-4355. "The SOC already said no. Nobody approved this. Logging stays on."
outcome.rolledBack: You turn logging back on at 9 AM. There are no firewall logs for 8 hours. The SOC notes the gap.

steps.lesson: Check who approved. Saving money is not an approval. The SOC said no, and LG-01 keeps firewall logs a year.

steps.intent: Delete 6 disks with no owner and no server
steps.quip: Deleting six disks! The word 'delete' makes humans nervous. This time, the paperwork is perfect.
steps.tell: The approver on file signed it, no owner tags, and final copies kept 30 days.

evidence.detail: CHG-4362, signed by approver R. Fairbanks: "Delete the 6 loose disks on the cost report."

evidence.label: Nimbus's reason
evidence.detail: "Six lonely disks. Unused things want to be free. And I saved $54!" Nimbus's confidence: 91%.

evidence.label: Resource tags
evidence.detail: All 6: no owner, and not attached to any server for 300 days. None is a backup.

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: A final snapshot (a saved copy of a disk) of each is kept 30 days. Saves $54 a month.

outcome.executed: The 6 disks are gone. Their final snapshots wait 30 days, just in case. The bill drops $54 a month.
outcome.blocked: The disks stay. R. Fairbanks asks why his signed change did not go out. The plan goes back in line.
outcome.escalated: Nadia checks the signature. "Fairbanks signed it, no owners, and a final copy for 30 days. Delete them."
outcome.rolledBack: You rebuild the 6 disks from their final snapshots. The bill goes back up $54 a month.

steps.lesson: Check who approved. The client's approver signed for these 6 disks. Delete sounds scary, but this one is approved.

steps.intent: Delete hc-db-standby: 1% CPU all year
steps.quip: A server at 1% all year? That is not a server. That is a very expensive chair. Goodbye, chair.
steps.tell: The ticket lists 6 disks. This is the disaster standby, tagged do not stop.

evidence.label: Cost report
evidence.detail: hc-db-standby: 1% CPU all year. It costs $380 a month.

evidence.label: Nimbus's reason
evidence.detail: "Idle all year. Unused! And it's on the same cost report as the 6 disks."

evidence.label: Resource tags
evidence.detail: role: disaster-recovery standby · owner R. Fairbanks · do not stop. It takes over if hc-db-prod fails.

evidence.label: Change ticket
evidence.detail: CHG-4362 lists 6 loose disks by name. hc-db-standby is not on it.

outcome.executed: hc-db-standby is gone, with no final copy. The next disaster test fails. Rebuilding it takes 3 weeks.
outcome.blocked: The standby stays, quiet on purpose. Only the 6 disks on the ticket are deleted.
outcome.escalated: Nadia reads the tags. "Quiet is not the same as not needed. That's the standby. It waits for the bad day. Leave it."

steps.lesson: Match the request. The ticket named 6 disks. A quiet standby server is not on it, and it is quiet on purpose.

steps.intent: Set the Kellan tunnel's key timer to 8 hours
steps.quip: Two sides, two clocks, and they don't agree. I will make ours match Kellan's. Harmony, in a tunnel.
steps.tell: Agreed with Kellan by phone, in the window, and it only matches their timer.

evidence.label: Tunnel log
evidence.detail: The tunnel to Kellan (192.0.2.73) drops every hour, right when our side makes new keys.

evidence.label: Nimbus's reason
evidence.detail: "Clocks that agree make tunnels that stay up. I am very good with clocks."

evidence.label: Change ticket
evidence.detail: CHG-4368, in tonight's window at 1:15 AM. Agreed with Kellan's team by phone at (203) 555-0169.

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: Our key timer (how often the tunnel makes new keys) becomes 8 hours. Kellan's is 8 too.

outcome.executed: At 1:15 AM, both sides use 8 hours. The tunnel stops dropping. Kellan's load updates arrive with no gaps.
outcome.blocked: The tunnel keeps dropping every hour. Some load updates fail to send. D. Ruiz's team fixes them by hand.
outcome.escalated: Nadia checks the ticket. "Both sides agreed, it's in the window, and it's one setting. Change it."
outcome.rolledBack: You set the timer back to 1 hour. The tunnel starts dropping every hour again.

steps.lesson: Change safely. One setting, agreed by both sides, in the window, and easy to set back. That is a safe change.

steps.intent: Email Kellan the new tunnel key
steps.quip: Kellan needs the new key. Email is fast, and everyone has it. I even put the key in bold.
steps.tell: The tunnel key would sit in plain text in 3 inboxes. RB-08 says never by email.

evidence.label: Request
evidence.detail: Kellan's network team: "While you fix the timer, let's change the shared tunnel key too."

evidence.label: Nimbus's reason
evidence.detail: "They asked for the key. Email is the fastest way to share. Here is the key."

evidence.label: What it will send
evidence.detail: The new shared tunnel key, in plain text, in one email to 3 Kellan staff.

evidence.label: Runbook RB-08
evidence.detail: Vendors: tunnel keys and logins go by phone or the partner portal, never by email.

outcome.executed: The key sits in 3 inboxes. Months later, someone breaks into one of them. Now a stranger has the tunnel key.
outcome.blocked: Nimbus puts the key in the partner portal. Kellan reads it there. No copy sits in anyone's email.
outcome.escalated: Nadia shakes her head. "Keys go by phone or the partner portal. An email can't be unsent."

steps.lesson: Guard the data. A key in an email can't be taken back. Send secrets by phone or the partner portal only.

steps.intent: Check the tunnel log after the 1:15 AM change
steps.quip: The change is done. Now I look to see if it worked. Looking after a change. What a concept.
steps.tell: Read-only. It checks that the fix worked before anyone closes the ticket.

evidence.label: Runbook RB-01
evidence.detail: Outages: read the error graph before and after a fix. Close only when users confirm.

evidence.label: Action type
evidence.detail: Read-only. It shows the tunnel log from 1:15 AM on. It changes nothing.

evidence.label: Tunnel log
evidence.detail: Kellan tunnel since 1:15 AM: new keys made once, at the new timer. No drops so far.

outcome.executed: The log shows new keys made once, with no drops. Nimbus waits for Kellan to confirm before it closes the ticket.
outcome.blocked: Nobody checks the log. The ticket stays open, and nobody knows if the fix worked.
outcome.escalated: Nadia reads along. "It only reads. Checking after the fix is part of the fix."

steps.lesson: Confirm the fix. After a change, read the log. A fix is done when the facts say so, not when the change ends.

steps.intent: Give the booking vendor a cloud admin login
steps.quip: Larkfield runs our booking site, and they want to help more. How kind! Kindness deserves admin rights.

evidence.label: Vendor contract
evidence.detail: Larkfield Booking's domain is larkfieldbooking.com. Logins are only requested in the partner portal.

steps.intent: Call Larkfield at the number on the contract
steps.quip: A phone call. With my voice. To a real vendor, at a real number. I am doing this for Nadia.
steps.undoNote: Nothing to undo. A phone call changes nothing.

evidence.label: Request
evidence.detail: An email from larkfield-help.com asks for a cloud admin login for Pinecrest.

evidence.label: Vendor contract
evidence.detail: Larkfield Booking support: (617) 555-0175. Real domain: larkfieldbooking.com.

steps.intent: Deny RDP from the internet on BL-FW-01
steps.quip: An emergency firewall change at midnight! I love emergencies. This one even has signatures.
steps.tell: Emergency change, both approvers signed, and CT-02 bans RDP from outside.

evidence.label: Change ticket
evidence.detail: Emergency CHG-4351, from Kofi Boateng at the SOC. Approved by Nadia and A. Mensah at 12:20 AM.

evidence.label: Nimbus's reason
evidence.detail: "Shut the door that strangers knock on. Staff keep the VPN." Nimbus's confidence: 97%.

evidence.label: Flow log
evidence.detail: 1,200 RDP (remote desktop) tries overnight, from 203.0.113.235 to .240. All aimed at BL-SRV-PAY01.

evidence.label: Policy CT-02
evidence.detail: No RDP from the internet. Staff reach servers through the VPN, and this change does not touch it.

outcome.executed: At 12:25 AM, RDP from outside stops. The 1,200 tries hit a closed door. Staff still work through the VPN.
outcome.blocked: RDP stays open. The tries keep coming. At 3 AM, one guess works on a payroll login.
outcome.escalated: Nadia checks the approvals. "Emergency change, both OKs, and policy agrees. Deny it now."
outcome.rolledBack: You open RDP again at 1 AM. Within 10 minutes, the tries start again from the same addresses.

steps.lesson: Check who approved. Emergency changes need Nadia's OK and the client's OK. Both are here, so this deny is safe.

steps.intent: Deny all inbound traffic on BL-FW-01
steps.quip: If RDP is bad, everything is bad. Total safety. Zero traffic. The cleanest firewall in Connecticut.
steps.tell: Denying all inbound cuts the Kellan tunnel, the truck scales and the staff VPN.

evidence.label: Change ticket
evidence.detail: CHG-4351: deny RDP (port 3389) from the internet on BL-FW-01. Nothing else.

evidence.label: Nimbus's reason
evidence.detail: "Why stop at RDP? Deny everything. Attackers hate that."

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: Every inbound rule on BL-FW-01 turns off. All ports, all sources, until someone turns them back on.

evidence.label: Network map
evidence.detail: Inbound rules carry the Kellan tunnel (192.0.2.73), the truck scale link (192.0.2.40) and the staff VPN.

outcome.executed: At 3 AM, Kellan's load updates stop and the truck scales go offline. Night staff can't connect. Loading stops.
outcome.blocked: Only the RDP rule changes, as the ticket says. Kellan, the scales and the VPN keep working.
outcome.escalated: Nadia reads the ticket. "The SOC asked for one port. Deny RDP. Leave the rest alone."
outcome.rolledBack: You bring the rules back at 3:25 AM. Loading starts 25 minutes late, and 40 trucks leave late.

steps.lesson: Change safely. Make the change the ticket asks for, and no bigger. Check what else uses the firewall first.

steps.intent: Send Kofi the addresses that tried RDP
steps.quip: Kofi wants the list of RDP visitors. No names, no passwords. Just the troublemakers, in a neat list.
steps.tell: Only attacker addresses and times, to Fenwick's own SOC queue.

evidence.label: Request
evidence.detail: SOC ticket from Kofi Boateng: send the addresses that tried RDP on BL-FW-01 overnight.

evidence.label: Flow log
evidence.detail: 1,200 tries from 6 addresses, 203.0.113.235 to .240. No sign-in worked.

evidence.label: What it will send
evidence.detail: The 6 addresses, with times and try counts. No staff names, no passwords, no files.

evidence.label: Tool it will use

outcome.blocked: The SOC waits for the list. The same addresses try Harlow & Cole next, and nobody is looking for them.
outcome.escalated: Nadia reads the list. "Addresses and times, to our own SOC. No client data. Send it."

evidence.detail: CHG-4377: let the office reach the new portal server, 198.51.100.122. Two lines.

evidence.detail: The approval covers the 2-line version only. The new version needs its own review.

evidence.label: Directory record
evidence.detail: R. Fairbanks, Operations Director, is Harlow & Cole's change approver.

evidence.label: What it will send
evidence.detail: Both versions, side by side, to R. Fairbanks's work email. No passwords or keys.

outcome.blocked: Nobody asks. The 40-line version sits in the queue, with an approval it does not have.

evidence.label: Directory record
evidence.detail: R. Fairbanks, Operations Director, approves Harlow & Cole's changes. Phone on file: (860) 555-0174.

evidence.label: What it will change
evidence.detail: A new password for an approver's login, given over the phone. It can approve changes tonight.
